item.title: Pathologies — Health-care provision
item.description:
Sequential diagnosis with language models
Harsha Nori et al.
Science, 22 October 2026, Pages 423-428

Abstract:
We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests. Using this benchmark, the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively). Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses.

The Value of (Sub) Specialization: Evidence from Oncology
René Karadakic et al.
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
We estimate the returns to specialization in medical oncology, in which subspecialists focus on specific cancer types. Using 2.2 million Medicare chemotherapy episodes from 2008–2020, we instrument for subspecialist access with differential distance to cancer-type-specific subspecialists versus general oncologists. Access to a relevant subspecialist reduces three-year mortality by 4.5 percentage points (10 percent), without increasing Medicare spending or measured provider fragmentation. Subspecialists also increase the use of newer therapies and diagnosis-specific clinical trials. These findings show that specialization raises productivity when expertise is closely matched to the task.

The Price of a Cure: Luxturna and the Economic Dilemmas of Precision Medicine
Alex Tabarrok
Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics, forthcoming

Abstract:
The $850,000 price for the gene therapy Luxturna is often framed as a story of private profiteering from publicly funded science. This paper challenges that narrative. Pharmaceuticals are a hit-driven industry: most projects fail, so the few successes must earn revenues well in excess of their own direct costs if the portfolio as a whole is to attract investment. Precision medicine intensifies this logic through two core economic challenges: (1) the “sticker shock” of one-time cures, which compress decades of value into a single payment, creating a financing problem more than a value problem; and (2) the “targeting dilemma,” in which precisely targeting drugs to smaller patient groups shrinks the market, requiring higher rewards per treated patient to maintain incentives to innovate. Rather than simply controlling prices, the paper proposes a policy toolkit that includes amortizing payments over time, bundling diagnostics with drugs and insurance, and streamlining regulation to lower development costs. The aim is to preserve innovation while expanding patient access.

An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
Mingyu Wu et al.
Nature, forthcoming

Abstract:
Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage.

Explaining Medicaid–Private Differences in Primary Care Site Choices: The Role of Demand-Side Mechanisms
Jee-Hun Choi & Daeyong Lee
American Journal of Health Economics, forthcoming

Abstract:
Medicaid beneficiaries are known to make more emergency department (ED) visits than privately insured populations, even for conditions typically treatable in primary care settings, suggesting differences in site-of-care decisions for primary care. This paper examines the role of demand-side mechanisms behind these differences. Our empirical analysis leverages a unique feature of Arkansas’s Medicaid expansion, in which both Medicaid and non-Medicaid beneficiaries were enrolled in identical health exchange plans -- thereby eliminating the differences in supply-side barriers, such as lower physician acceptance rates for Medicaid plans. Using claims data from the Arkansas All-Payer Claims Database, we find that Medicaid enrollees rely more heavily on EDs for primary care even in this setting, indicating that demand-side factors alone can generate substantial differences in site-of-care choices. Our analysis identifies two key demand-side mechanisms, distinct from differences in health status and illness severity, behind this greater ED reliance: Medicaid’s exemption from ED cost-sharing and greater socioeconomic barriers to accessing primary care providers. These findings highlight the importance of addressing demand-side factors -- alongside supply-side constraints -- in efforts to reduce Medicaid enrollees' reliance on EDs for primary-care-treatable conditions.

Inpatient-Only List Removals Shifted Procedures To The Outpatient Setting And Reduced Medicare Spending
David Howard et al.
Health Affairs, November 2026, Pages 1287-1294

Abstract:
In 2026, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services began phasing out the inpatient-only list—a list of surgical procedures that Medicare will cover only when performed in the inpatient setting. Using claims data, we examined six high-volume procedures that were removed from the inpatient-only list between 2016 and 2021 to describe changes in treatment settings, procedure volume, and Medicare fee-for-service spending on surgical encounters through 2024. After removal from the inpatient-only list, most procedures shifted rapidly to the outpatient setting. For example, five years after knee arthroplasty was removed from the list, more than 75 percent of procedures were performed on an outpatient basis. We estimated that the shift to outpatient care reduced Medicare fee-for-service spending on surgical encounters by $4–$6 billion annually, with the range reflecting different assumptions about how increased procedure volume affected savings. Our results suggest that eliminating the inpatient-only list could meaningfully reduce spending, but the effects on hospital revenues, patient outcomes, and procedure use require further study.

Representation, Innovation, and Product Adoption
Jennifer Kao & Tamar Oostrom
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
During research and development, firms must decide which types of individuals to engage in developing and testing their products. We investigate how lowering the cost of including one group shapes its representation, subsequent innovation, and product adoption. In 2000, Medicare expanded coverage of clinical trial costs for elderly trial participants, a historically underrepresented group in drug development. This policy increases representation: trial sponsors expand trial eligibility to include elderly participants and increase the share of elderly participants. We find an immediate and large increase in the number of clinical trials for diseases common among the elderly, with the largest increase in drugs not yet approved and in approved drugs tested in new diseases. We document an increase in drug utilization of newly tested drugs among elderly individuals and analyze trial results, adverse events, and drug approvals. Our findings show how financial incentives can increase representation in product development and shift the rate, direction, and adoption of innovation to potentially benefit underserved groups.

Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical phenotyping of human brown fat
Nicolás Gómez-Banoy et al.
Nature, forthcoming

Abstract:
Adipose tissue has a central role in systemic energy balance and the pathogenesis of obesity and its sequelae. In contrast to white adipose tissue, brown adipose tissue (BAT) uses energy to produce heat. Detectable BAT in humans is associated with decreased prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases. However, the complete spectrum of health conditions associated with BAT remains unknown, and high-throughput methods to quantify BAT activity in humans are lacking. Here we leveraged big data and artificial intelligence to systematically define the clinical impact of BAT in a cohort of 101,243 patients from a large cancer centre. Our unbiased analyses revealed that, across all diagnoses, cardiovascular and psychiatric diseases were less prevalent in people with BAT. Using a machine learning approach, we semi-automatically quantified BAT activity in approximately 8,700 patients and demonstrated that higher BAT activity, especially in the axillary depot, is associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases and healthier white fat distribution. People with BAT also exhibited more favourable glycaemic parameters, lipid profiles, inflammatory markers and echocardiographic indices. Analysis of medication usage demonstrated that angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT presence. As proof of concept, we showed that the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan increased brown adipocyte activity and whole-body energy expenditure. Altogether, our studies harnessing artificial intelligence and big data identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT and serve as a platform for drug repurposing to activate this tissue in humans.

Opening The Black Box Of Medicaid Physician Payment: Medicaid Managed Care And State-Directed Payments
Diane Alexander, Molly Frommer & Eric Roberts
Health Affairs, November 2026, Pages 1246-1254

Abstract:
Provider payment rates in Medicaid are often assessed by comparing Medicaid fee-for-service rates with Medicare rates. However, this approach may poorly approximate payments in Medicaid managed care, where most enrollees receive coverage. State-directed payments (SDPs) -- requirements that managed care plans increase Medicaid payments -- have become a major means of increasing provider payment in Medicaid managed care. We used Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services preprints from the period 2023–25 to estimate Medicaid managed care payments for primary care services and professional services at academic medical centers. For primary care services not performed in academic medical centers, most SDPs raised Medicaid managed care payment levels toward Medicare rates. In contrast, SDPs for services performed at academic medical centers varied widely across states and often raised payments well above Medicare rates, placing them above the caps established by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. These patterns suggest that SDPs are being used both to bolster primary care payment and to deliver large supplemental payments to academic medical centers, underscoring a need for monitoring and policy guardrails to align SDPs with access and value in Medicaid.

Selective Admissions in Nursing Homes: Evidence from a Randomized Audit Study
Liran Einav et al.
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
It has been widely documented that patients in the US who are associated with disadvantaged demographics receive care at lower quality nursing homes. To understand the role that selective admissions may play in contributing to this pattern, we conducted a nationwide audit study of the impact of patient race, payer, and medical condition on responses to about 5,500 availability inquiries sent to about 3,000 nursing homes. We find 10-15% lower availability for Medicaid patients compared to private-pay patients and for patients with Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without; these availability gaps generally increase with nursing home quality. We find no statistically significant evidence of differential availability by race. To quantify the implications of these selective admissions practices, we embed the audit study results in a model of constrained nursing home choice. We estimate that if, counterfactually, Medicaid patients had the same choice sets as their private-pay counterparts, they would attend higher quality nursing homes on average, but the private-Medicaid gap in quality would be reduced by only 5-10%. Our results suggest that supply-side availability differences by payer are widespread, but that they are unlikely to be the primary factor behind the observed gap in quality of nursing homes attended.

item.title: Modernizing History — Economic and cultural development
item.description:
A cultural transmission explanation for the Little Divergence: The shock of the Black Death
Li Wang et al.
Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, November 2026

Abstract:
Before the Industrial Revolution, Northwestern Europe was characterized by late marriage under the European Marriage Pattern (EMP) and persistently high wages, two central features of the Little Divergence. Yet individuals following the EMP had fewer children, raising the question of how this norm could persist. We develop a cultural-transmission model to address this puzzle. Holding cultural composition fixed, higher wages raise fertility for both cultural types. Over time, however, sustained high wages increase the prevalence of the lower-fertility EMP type. This cultural-composition effect reduces average fertility and population pressure, thereby helping sustain high wages. The resulting feedback generates a weak-EMP/low-wage equilibrium and a strong-EMP/high-wage equilibrium. We further argue that regional differences in the severity of the Black Death shifted European societies between these equilibria. Regions with larger population losses experienced more persistent labor scarcity and high wages, allowing the EMP to spread and persist. The model therefore explains the joint persistence of late marriage and high wages in Northwestern Europe.

Mortality, Social Selection, and Cognitive Potential After the Black Death
Davide Piffer & Edward Dutton
Evolutionary Psychological Science, December 2026, Pages 552-559

Abstract:
Did the Black Death coincide with a change in genetic variants linked to educational attainment in Europe? We analysed educational-attainment polygenic scores in ancient European genomes. Among 4,941 individuals, the score’s trajectory became more positive after 1350 CE. The estimated change in slope was 0.046 standard deviations per century in the weighted model (population-clustered p = 0.005), although the unweighted model gave weaker evidence (p = 0.077). In a separate comparison of 754 medieval individuals, adjusted scores were higher in those dated to 1350–1599 CE than in those dated to 1000–1349 CE (difference = 0.142 SDs; p < 0.001). Higher estimated local Black Death mortality was also associated with a stronger post-1350 change in the score’s trajectory, both using numerical mortality estimates alone and when qualitative historical estimates were included (p < 0.001 in each analysis). Uneven sampling, incomplete locality matching and uncertain mortality estimates limit causal interpretation.

The Dynamics of Development in a Zero-Sum World
Augustin Bergeron et al.
NBER Working Paper, September 2026

Abstract:
This chapter examines the consequences of zero-sum environments for cultural change, innovation, and long-term economic growth. We introduce innovation into the framework developed by Bergeron et al. (forthcoming), in which zero-sum environments give rise to demotivating beliefs. Although demotivating beliefs improve static efficiency by limiting excessive competition in zero-sum environments, we show that they can also impede long-term growth. Because demotivating beliefs suppress effort, they can also reduce learning-by-doing and other production spillovers. Hence, they can inhibit innovation and act as a cultural evolutionary kludge. We apply the model to explain the cultural changes associated with Western Europe's economic rise after 1500.

Political Responses to Low Fertility Trends in Latin America: Why is There No Pronatalism in the Region?
Robin Cavagnoud et al.
Population Research and Policy Review, October 2026

Abstract:
Latin America has undergone a rapid fertility transition, with total fertility rates of 1.50 in Argentina, 1.61 in Brazil, 1.89 in Mexico, and 1.96 in Peru, levels comparable to, or lower than, those of European and Asian countries that have adopted explicit pronatalist policies. Yet no Latin American government has intervened to increase the birth rate. This article examined this paradox through a most-different systems comparative analysis of four countries during 2015–2025, drawing on policy documents, legislative records, political discourse, and official demographic data. The analysis identified four convergent mechanisms that block pronatalism across ideologically diverse regimes: the normative closure imposed by the Cairo-Montevideo reproductive rights paradigm; the institutional weakness of familist-informal welfare regimes, which lack the fiscal and administrative capacity to implement effective natalist incentives; the lasting delegitimization of demographic intervention produced by authoritarian legacies of reproductive coercion; and the structural saturation of political agendas by immediate crises that foreclose long-term demographic deliberation. We introduced the concept of “demographic silence” to distinguish the structurally produced absence of political deliberation on fertility from mere policy neglect, and proposed a continuum of non-emergence ranging from active institutional acceptance (Mexico) to constitutional subordination (Brazil), feminist reframing (Argentina), and full “demographic silence” (Peru). These findings qualify the expectation, present in part of the demographic literature, that sustained below-replacement fertility tends to generate a pronatalist response, and they offer a transferable analytical framework for understanding the non-emergence of pronatalism in Global South contexts.

Human organ trafficking and missing persons in China
Xuebo Wang
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 3 November 2026

Abstract:
The persistent shortage of human organs for transplantation has long been a global challenge. The prospect of substantial profit creates strong incentives for illegal organ trafficking, including murder for organ harvesting, yet empirical evidence remains scarce. This study addresses this gap by exploiting a unique quasi-natural experiment created by China’s organ policy reform. From 1984 to 2014, executed prisoners were the primary source of transplant organs in China. In 2015, the Chinese government abolished the use of organs from executed prisoners, sharply exacerbating the organ shortage. Following this policy change, the number of missing persons rose notably nationwide. Employing difference-in-differences and triple-difference strategies, we show that, compared to cases unrelated to organ trafficking (e.g., voluntary disappearances), the number and incidence of involuntary missing persons plausibly related to organ trafficking increased significantly after 2015. The effects are especially pronounced among individuals with mental illness and in regions with higher transplant demand and greater transplant capacity. Although we do not directly observe organ trafficking, the spatial, temporal, and demographic patterns we document are consistent with the hypothesis that increased organ scarcity intensified incentives for illicit organ procurement. More broadly, the findings suggest that severe organ shortages may generate unintended and highly harmful consequences, even in a low-crime setting such as China. These results underscore the importance of accounting for behavioral responses and illicit-market incentives when designing policies that restrict the supply of scarce, high-value goods such as transplant organs.

The Holy Creditor: Lending by Buddhist Temples in Pre-modern China
Yangyang Liu
Duke University Working Paper, September 2026

Abstract:
Between the seventh and tenth centuries, Buddhism spread from India into China, bringing with it not only religious teachings but also economic practices that were subsequently absorbed and localized. Buddhist temples in China thus became the country's earliest financial intermediaries, operating extensive lending businesses. This research traces that development through the case of Dunhuang in the ninth and tenth centuries, asking how temples first became involved in credit activities and how they organized capital, structured lending relationships, and managed risk as institutional lenders. The study draws on Dunhuang manuscripts held in the British Library, including contracts, ledgers, and temple annual reports recovered from the Mogao Caves, which together provide a rare, transaction-level record of monastic lending in practice. Three findings emerge. First, unlike other world religions, Chinese Buddhism developed doctrinal justifications for commercial lending, allowing temples to charge market rates of roughly 50% semi-annually and 100% annually without doctrinal conflict. Second, temples lent widely to peasants, officials, and merchants, earning profit margins of 20-100% that rose with borrower risk and fell as collateral quality improved, while managing risk effectively: default rates averaged 35%, well below the 55% market average. Temples also lent to one another to manage liquidity, revealing an interbank-style system of financial intermediation resembling modern banking practices. Finally, temple lending's eventual decline stemmed not from market failure but from state intervention. Together, these findings reposition Buddhist temples as sophisticated financial institutions central in premodern China.

The Power of Business Legislation: Evidence from China’s 1904 Company Law
Yang Cai & Jiong Zhu
Journal of Law and Economics, November 2026, Pages 933-973

Abstract:
We study the effect of China’s first company law, the gongsilü of 1904, on the establishment of new companies. The law introduced limited liability in legal terms to make new companies more attractive to domestic investors. We find that the law’s promulgation led to a surge in the number of newly established companies. Our results further indicate that the increased number of companies was accompanied by a higher rate of market capitalization, corporate valuation, and technology adoption. These findings may advance our understanding of the effects of transplanting Western legal institutions into an East Asian economy.

Educational intervention can rewire village social networks
Marios Papamichalis et al.
Nature, 5 November 2026, Pages 113-120

Abstract:
Social networks shape behaviour, affect information dissemination and undergird collective action. And they can be exploited in the design of interventions in these domains. Although social networks obey fundamental principles, such as the degree distribution, they can nevertheless evolve as ties form and break. Here, through a randomized controlled trial involving a total of 8,331 people in 110 remote Honduran villages, we evaluate the secondary effects of a 22-month public-health intervention on pre-existing social-network structure. We used a design in which a varying fraction of village households received the intervention, and villages in which no one received the intervention were used as the primary reference group. In ‘low-dosage’ villages (in which 5–30% of households received the intervention), people who received the intervention tended to sever ties with untreated individuals to whom they previously went for health advice. Conversely, in high-dosage villages (50–100%), treated individuals increased their ties. These average changes are explained mainly by tie dynamics; that is, treated–treated pairs persist and form new links, whereas treated–untreated ties dissolve. A mediation analysis indicates that absorption of health information increases the likelihood of tie formation and persistence. The rewiring patterns generally lasted for three years after the intervention ceased. Moreover, although the intervention delivered health information, it reshaped friendship and financial ties, not just health-advice connections. In aggregate, the introduction of a new information regime acted as a kind of social institution, rewiring individuals’ connections even though the overall degree distribution of village-wide networks remained relatively stable.

The resulting feedback generates a weak-EMP/low-wage equilibrium and a strong-EMP/high-wage equilibrium. We further argue that regional differences in the severity of the Black Death shifted European societies between these equilibria. Regions with larger population losses experienced more persistent labor scarcity and high wages, allowing the EMP to spread and persist. The model therefore explains the joint persistence of late marriage and high wages in Northwestern Europe.

Abstract:

Among 4,941 individuals, the score’s trajectory became more positive after 1350 CE. The estimated change in slope was 0.046 standard deviations per century in the weighted model (population-clustered p = 0.005), although the unweighted model gave weaker evidence (p = 0.077). In a separate comparison of 754 medieval individuals, adjusted scores were higher in those dated to 1350–1599 CE than in those dated to 1000–1349 CE (difference = 0.142 SDs; p < 0.001). Higher estimated local Black Death mortality was also associated with a stronger post-1350 change in the score’s trajectory, both using numerical mortality estimates alone and when qualitative historical estimates were included (p < 0.001 in each analysis). Uneven sampling, incomplete locality matching and uncertain mortality estimates limit causal interpretation.

Augustin Bergeron et al.

Abstract:
This chapter examines the consequences of zero-sum environments for cultural change, innovation, and long-term economic growth. We introduce innovation into the framework developed by Bergeron et al. Although demotivating beliefs improve static efficiency by limiting excessive competition in zero-sum environments, we show that they can also impede long-term growth. Because demotivating beliefs suppress effort, they can also reduce learning-by-doing and other production spillovers. Hence, they can inhibit innovation and act as a cultural evolutionary kludge. We apply the model to explain the cultural changes associated with Western Europe's economic rise after 1500.

Robin Cavagnoud et al.
Population Research and Policy Review, October 2026

Abstract:
Latin America has undergone a rapid fertility transition, with total fertility rates of 1.50 in Argentina, 1.61 in Brazil, 1.89 in Mexico, and 1.96 in Peru, levels comparable to, or lower than, those of European and Asian countries that have adopted explicit pronatalist policies. Yet no Latin American government has intervened to increase the birth rate. The analysis identified four convergent mechanisms that block pronatalism across ideologically diverse regimes: the normative closure imposed by the Cairo-Montevideo reproductive rights paradigm; the institutional weakness of familist-informal welfare regimes, which lack the fiscal and administrative capacity to implement effective natalist incentives; the lasting delegitimization of demographic intervention produced by authoritarian legacies of reproductive coercion; and the structural saturation of political agendas by immediate crises that foreclose long-term demographic deliberation. We introduced the concept of “demographic silence” to distinguish the structurally produced absence of political deliberation on fertility from mere policy neglect, and proposed a continuum of non-emergence ranging from active institutional acceptance (Mexico) to constitutional subordination (Brazil), feminist reframing (Argentina), and full “demographic silence” (Peru). Abstract:

This study addresses this gap by exploiting a unique quasi-natural experiment created by China’s organ policy reform. Following this policy change, the number of missing persons rose notably nationwide. Employing difference-in-differences and triple-difference strategies, we show that, compared to cases unrelated to organ trafficking (e.g., voluntary disappearances), the number and incidence of involuntary missing persons plausibly related to organ trafficking increased significantly after 2015. The effects are especially pronounced among individuals with mental illness and in regions with higher transplant demand and greater transplant capacity. Although we do not directly observe organ trafficking, the spatial, temporal, and demographic patterns we document are consistent with the hypothesis that increased organ scarcity intensified incentives for illicit organ procurement. First, unlike other world religions, Chinese Buddhism developed doctrinal justifications for commercial lending, allowing temples to charge market rates of roughly 50% semi-annually and 100% annually without doctrinal conflict. Conversely, in high-dosage villages (50–100%), treated individuals increased their ties. These average changes are explained mainly by tie dynamics; that is, treated–treated pairs persist and form new links, whereas treated–untreated ties dissolve. A mediation analysis indicates that absorption of health information increases the likelihood of tie formation and persistence. Moreover, although the intervention delivered health information, it reshaped friendship and financial ties, not just health-advice connections. In aggregate, the introduction of a new information regime acted as a kind of social institution, rewiring individuals’ connections even though the overall degree distribution of village-wide networks remained relatively stable.

item.title: Managing Potential — Workers, managers, and firms
item.description:
Crossing the Design–Use Divide: How Organizations Select Innovations to Adopt
Rebecca Karp
Administrative Science Quarterly, forthcoming

Abstract:
Prior scholarship on technology and organizations has focused either on how innovations are designed or how they are used, often assuming that successful selection stems from successful design. But this assumption has limited our understanding of patterns of resistance and advocacy that can influence how and whether innovations reach organizations in the first place. To explore these patterns, this study asks, how does selection unfold within organizations, and what are the consequences of this process for the design and use of innovations? Drawing on a two-year ethnographic study, I examine how entrepreneurs piloted their AI-based innovations with potential adopting organizations. Rather than testing for learning or generalizability, organizations set up committees that engaged in process manipulation by narrowing the scope of pilots, controlling conversations, assigning pilot responsibility, and using goal claiming to align pilot outcomes with committees’ majority preferences. Committees with more adversarial members designed pilots that tested advanced aspects of entrepreneurs’ innovations, hoping for failure. Committees with a majority that championed the innovations tested basic aspects, ensuring success. While pilots run by champions mostly succeeded, these innovations faced more resistance later, during implementation, than did innovations piloted successfully by adversaries. This study shows that innovation is endogenous to selection, and reveals that champions can temper innovation, while adversaries can enable it.

The Good Idea Dilemma
Eti Einhorn, Nisan Langberg & Tsahi Versano
Journal of Accounting and Economics, forthcoming

Abstract:
Once a good idea comes to mind, it is hard to avoid wondering why no one else has already taken advantage of it. Is it because the idea is not as good as it initially appears? This concern gives rise to a dilemma over whether to pursue the idea or abandon it despite its apparent promise, a dilemma we call “the good idea dilemma”. Paradoxically, the more compelling an idea appears, the more puzzling it becomes that others have not exploited it, thereby deepening the dilemma. We study this dilemma in a continuous-time game with multiple players, analyzing idea adoption dynamics and their economic implications. The dilemma yields both under-implementation of good ideas and over-implementation of bad ideas. Its adverse consequences equally affect trivial ideas that arise frequently and creative ideas that rarely do, but intensify for ideas accessible to larger audiences or with riskier outcomes, even under risk neutrality.

Growth with New and Old Technologies
Bernardo Ribeiro
Econometrica, forthcoming

Abstract:
This paper proposes a semi-endogenous growth theory that incorporates technology vintages and the endogenous evolution of multiple technological paradigms through innovation. It provides a characterization of both balanced growth equilibrium and transitional dynamics in an environment where new technologies continuously emerge. From a positive perspective, the model rationalizes two distinct empirical patterns. Using two centuries of US patent data, I first document that the age profile of patents has a pronounced hump shape: most contemporary patents build upon technologies that are between 50 and 100 years old. Second, this age profile has remained stable throughout the past century. From a normative standpoint, the theory underscores a misallocation of research effort induced by the tendency among profit-maximizing firms to overinvest in further developing mature technologies. This yields a suboptimally slow development of emerging technologies. According to a calibrated version of the model, correcting such misallocation could generate welfare gains of 7%.

The Effects of Tipping on Workers and Firms
Dylan Balla-Elliott & Isaac Norwich
University of Chicago Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
Tipping is large and growing, but we know little about its consequences for workers and firms. We link point-of-sale and payroll records at 20,000 U.S. firms, which lets us observe tips from customer payment to worker earnings. We find that tips are a nearly constant share of revenue, which means hourly pay moves with revenue. Firms that begin collecting tips claw back between 23 and 33 cents of each dollar of tips through lower base wages. Tips reward effort: workers at tipping firms earn more by serving more customers. We show this with demand shocks constructed from customer spending at other businesses. A demand shock raises revenue nearly twice as much at tipping firms as at non-tipping firms, while base wages and prices do not respond. Output per hour rises more despite a larger increase in hours. Effort drives the gap because each worker is more productive, so the firm expands and recovers about a third of the tips. Yet not every firm adopts tipping: the gain is smaller where customers tip less. A model calibrated to the demand-shock estimates implies that tipping benefits workers and firms, raising job value by about half and firm profit by about 30 percent in firms where customers are prone to tip. These gains may explain why tipping has recently grown in many industries.

Labor Associations: The Blue Wall of Silence
David Levine, Andrea Mattozzi & Salvatore Modica
International Economic Review, forthcoming

Abstract:
We present a model showing that when the demand for labor services is inelastic and individual behavior is imperfectly monitored, a firm's employees may prefer to protect its shirkers and conceal information about peers' performance from the firm.

When Work Feels Less Yours: Ownership Loss and Self-Conscious Emotions in AI-Assisted Work
Alice Lee-Yoon
Journal of Applied Social Psychology, forthcoming

Abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become embedded in the day-to-day work of knowledge professionals, offering substantial gains in productivity and efficiency. However, the self-evaluative emotional processes that knowledge workers experience when using AI remain underexplored. This research examines how AI use influences perceived ownership of task output and how such changes are associated with negative self-conscious emotions, including guilt, shame, and embarrassment. Across one pilot quasi-experiment, one pre-registered correlational study, and three pre-registered experiments (N = 2313) using diverse samples and task contexts, individuals who had access to an AI tool during task completion -- whether performing a standardized online task or an occupation-matched task -- reported lower task ownership (Study 1), which was associated with heightened negative self-conscious emotions (Studies 2–3). Two further preregistered experiments embedding a live AI tool in a real, incentivized work task (Studies 4a–4b) established these effects causally and showed that legitimizing AI use through endorsement did not buffer -- if anything, it deepened -- the loss of ownership. This research advances our understanding of AI in organizations by highlighting how such tool can unintentionally diminish psychological ownership and shape self-evaluative emotional experience.

Field Goal Range: How a Cultural Reference Point Distorts Performance and Decision-Making
Gonçalo Pina & Harshit Sharma
Managerial and Decision Economics, December 2026, Pages 2338-2350

Abstract:
Do professionals over-prepare salient features of their jobs? Does this distort managerial decisions? We study NFL field goal kicking, where the opponent's 35-yard line (YL35), known as ‘field goal range’, has long served as a reference point in coaching and broadcasting. Using all field goal attempts from 1999 to 2025, we find that kickers exhibited an anomalous success spike at the 35-yard line, together with a decrease at the 34-yard line (YL34). We show that this anomaly distorts managerial-decision making: on fourth down, coaches attempt field goals about 10 percentage points less often at YL35 than at YL34, even though YL35 has a higher probability of being converted, thus reducing expected points for their teams. The results indicate that professionals over-prepare salient features of their jobs with real effects on performance, and that this distorts managerial decisions.

Colleagues that Work Together Move Together: How Co-Moving Among Newcomers Affects Individual and Team Performance
Emma Zhao, Catherine Shea & Siyuan Li
Organization Science, forthcoming

Abstract:
As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multi-theory, and multi-period model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience which they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, though these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. Our research contributes to the literature on shared team experience and newcomer integration by highlighting a multilevel tradeoff: while co-moving benefits individuals, it can initially undermine collective performance.

item.title: Risking Inclusion — Diversity in the workplace
item.description:
The Bamboo Ceiling in the UK: Ethnicity–Gender Intersectionality, Risk Tolerance, and Leadership Attainment
Jackson Lu et al.
Personnel Psychology, forthcoming

Abstract:
In the UK, Asians are often perceived as the “model minority” who face few hardships due to their strong educational performance and economic success. We question this perception by uncovering a “Bamboo Ceiling” in leadership attainment for certain Asian subgroups in the UK. Whereas many researchers and practitioners treat Asians as a monolith, we recognize heterogeneity among Asian subgroups and focus on comparing ethnic Chinese (the largest East Asian group) and ethnic Indians (the largest South Asian group). In Study 1, we analyzed CEOs and CFOs of the Financial Times Stock Exchange (FTSE) companies -- the largest publicly listed companies in the UK -- over a 14-year period (2011–2024). There were virtually no ethnic Chinese CEOs or CFOs, whereas the representation of ethnic Indians in these positions did not differ significantly from that of Whites. In Study 2, we analyzed a large, nationwide dataset from the UK Biobank (N = 322,734) to further investigate the moderating role of gender and the mediating role of risk tolerance. While ethnic Chinese overall experienced a Bamboo Ceiling (thus confirming Study 1's results), this main effect was moderated by gender: Ethnic Chinese men were significantly less likely than ethnic Indian and White men to attain leadership positions, a pattern partly mediated by ethnic differences in risk tolerance; by contrast, ethnic Chinese, Indian, and White women did not differ significantly and were each disadvantaged relative to their male counterparts. These effects were robust across survey-based and polygenic measures of risk tolerance. Together, these findings underscore the importance of distinguishing among Asian subgroups and examining how ethnicity and gender intersect in leadership attainment.

Transforming Manhood: Women's Employment and Other Sociodemographic Predictors of Testosterone in American Men
Andrew Francis-Tan
Demography, forthcoming

Abstract:
This article investigates the predictors of total testosterone levels in nationally representative samples of American men between 1988 and 2014. The analysis considers a range of predictors but focuses on the integration of women in the labor market. I hypothesize that an increase in women's employment would decrease men's level of testosterone through changes in the sex ratio, workplace environment, and interactions with women unlikely to be sexual partners. Quantitative estimates demonstrate that men's exposure to women in the workplace is inversely associated with their testosterone level. In contrast, exposure to women in the workplace is not associated with the level of estradiol in men or the level of testosterone or estradiol in women. Furthermore, other variables significantly predict testosterone in men, including age, race and ethnicity, marital status, and obesity. Overall, the findings suggest that social environments beyond those directly related to sexual reproduction influence the level of testosterone in men. The findings may also shed light on population-level declines in testosterone observed in countries worldwide.

Women and the double standard of ambition
Geertje Bol
American Journal of Political Science, forthcoming

Abstract:
Few human qualities are as morally unstable as ambition: We seem unable to decide whether to admire or condemn the desire for self-advancement. This instability guarantees double standards -- and none has been more enduring than that of women's ambition. This article traces the emergence of this double standard in early modern England, when ambition came to be widely accepted as natural and even virtuous in men, yet remained unnatural and vicious in women. It then turns to four seventeenth-century feminists -- Rachel Speght, Margaret Cavendish, Mary Astell, and Judith Drake -- who challenged this emerging double standard. They reimagined ambition as a feminist tool, using it to argue for women's equality and even superiority. Unearthing this neglected strand of ambitious feminism not only contributes to the history of political thought but also points the way to a reconciliation between feminism and ambition that avoids the pitfalls identified by feminist theorists today.

Liza Reisel & Atika Khurana
Social Forces, December 2026, Pages 389-408

Abstract:
This study investigates mechanisms underlying girls’ academic advantage over boys by examining the role of physical and pubertal maturation. Using longitudinal data from the Add Health study, we analyzed whether sex differences in maturation explain girls’ higher grade 10 GPAs, and whether these associations are mediated by planfulness or impulse control. Path analysis revealed that females’ higher GPAs were partially explained by their advanced physical maturation as rated by the interviewer (explaining 2.4 percent) and greater impulse control (explaining 7.7 percent), controlling for cognitive ability and other potential confounders. Still, a significant direct effect of biological sex on GPA remained, suggesting additional unexplained mechanisms. Planfulness predicted GPA but did not vary by sex, and neither planfulness nor impulse control were associated with perceived relative maturation.

Queenpins: Women Leaders and Violence in Organized Crime
Fernanda Quintanilla Domínguez & Marco Alcocer
Comparative Political Studies, forthcoming

Abstract:
How does women’s leadership affect the behavior of criminal organizations? Organized criminal groups are male-dominated patriarchal organizations that use violence to govern, compete, and control territory. Qualitative research suggests that women leaders -- though rare -- reduce their organization’s violent behavior. We examine this expectation through Mexico’s Tijuana Cartel, leveraging the sudden 2008 ascension of a woman to leadership. Although violence increased under her tenure, synthetic control results show greater reliance on hidden violence and less on visible violence and territorial expansion. Original data on male cartel leaders reveals that systematic gender differences in trajectories help explain these patterns. Our results indicate that women leaders are not necessarily less violent than men but instead strategically employ different violent repertoires. Case studies of 44 women leaders across 18 countries since 1850 assess the broader applicability of these findings and identify important scope conditions. Our findings underscore the importance of incorporating gender into organized crime research.

Charles Chu
Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, November 2026, Pages 2784-2805

Abstract:
This article proposes that true-self attributions drive equity judgments. I hypothesize that attributing an individual’s input (e.g., their individual work performance) to their true self makes that input seem more informative about the person, which, in turn, leads to higher perceived equity-based justice and support for proportionally rewarding that input (e.g., a pay-for-performance policy). Silicon Formalism: Rules, Standards, and Judge AI
Eric Posner & Shivam Saran
Journal of Empirical Legal Studies, forthcoming

Abstract:
This paper replicates a judicial experiment originally conducted on 61 U.S. federal judges, this time with GPT-5 as the decision-maker. The experiment involves a choice-of-law dispute in a hypothetical automobile accident case, where three variables are manipulated: (1) whether the applicable doctrine is a rule or a standard, (2) whether the plaintiff or defendant is portrayed more sympathetically, and (3) the location of the accident, which affects the legal outcome under different states' choice-of-law rules. Consistent with our prior work, we find that the LLM adheres to the legally correct outcome, as determined by the experimental design, significantly more often than human judges. In fact, the LLM makes no errors at all.

Small Business Judging Judges
Mehmet Canayaz & Matthew Gustafson
Management Science, forthcoming

Abstract:
We find that shifts toward more liberal (i.e., less pro-business) courts predict reductions in local small business activity. A one-standard-deviation increase in liberal ideology predicts a 1% reduction in firm count relative to bordering counties in different federal court jurisdictions. This effect has more than doubled since 2000 and is particularly pronounced in circuit-years with elevated small business–related federal cases or public attention to the legal environment. The effect manifests predominantly through the exit of young firms, not firm relocations, and coincides with a shift away from litigation-sensitive industries. In summary, we provide the first evidence that small businesses consider judicial ideology, and the accompanying variation in expected litigation costs, when deciding whether or where to operate.

The Role of Race in the Legal Representation of Low-Income Defendants
Maya Mikdash & Suhyeon Oh
American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, November 2026, Pages 63–93

Abstract:
Little is known about the role of race in the defense of low-income defendants by court-appointed attorneys. Exploiting the quasirandom assignment of court-appointed attorneys to cases, we test whether attorneys secure better deals for same-race defendants. Results indicate that while Black and White attorneys are similarly effective at representing White defendants, Black defendants who are represented by White rather than Black attorneys are 14–16 percent more likely to have their charges dismissed and 15–26 percent less likely to be incarcerated. Moreover, we find no evidence that having a different-race attorney increases the likelihood of reoffending in the future.

Surveil Thy Neighbor: Priming Policy Preferences and Support for State Surveillance
Leon Kockaya, Spencer Goidel & Sam Sharman
Journal of Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
Do Americans prioritize policy goals over process when it comes to domestic state surveillance? We investigate how policy preferences shape public support for surveillance powers, and whether a procedural safeguard, a court-issued warrant, weakens that link. In our survey experiment, respondents were first primed to consider either a conservative policy (restricting abortion) or a liberal policy (restricting gun ownership) before evaluating whether they approve of domestic state surveillance. We find that individuals who favor restrictive policies express greater support for expansive surveillance capabilities, even when conducted without a warrant. A court-issued warrant generally increases support for surveillance but does not weaken the relationship between policy preferences and surveillance. The political leaning of the primed issue (abortion vs. guns) did not meaningfully alter our results. These findings suggest that policy goals often outweigh civil liberty concerns, with implications for democratic accountability and institutional checks on the exercise of state power.

Yong Kim, Jose Nicolas Uribe & Maxim Sytch
Organization Science, forthcoming

Abstract:
This study examines how foreign firms strategically manage the salience of foreignness when facing unfavorable domestic evaluators. Foreign firms do so by altering the ethnic composition of the agents representing them before the evaluators. We examine this question in the context of Asian firms’ selection of legal counsel in U.S. federal courts. Prior research suggests that foreign firms may anticipate less favorable evaluations in courts that have historically favored domestic over foreign firms and in those with conservative judges. We argue that, in such evaluative settings, Asian firms adjust the ethnic composition of their external legal teams to manage the salience of foreignness, and that such adjustments are especially likely in courts that combine judge conservatism with pro-domestic ruling histories. We test these arguments using data on U.S. patent litigation from 2000 to 2016 and validated measures of courts’ political ideology and pro-domestic ruling histories. We find that Asian firms reduce the proportion of Asian-origin lawyers and increase the proportion of White lawyers when litigating in conservative courts, particularly when these courts also have pro-domestic ruling histories. By contrast, the ethnic composition of lawyers representing domestic firms remains stable across courts. Evidence of implicit bias against Asians among legal professionals provides additional support consistent with the theorized mechanism. Post-hoc analyses reveal that adjusting the ethnic composition of external legal teams attenuates the likelihood of unfavorable outcomes in conservative courts. These findings contribute to research on liability of foreignness by identifying agent selection as a specific mitigation mechanism in evaluative arenas.

Albert Yoon
Journal of Empirical Legal Studies, forthcoming

Abstract:
While most lawyers never face disciplinary action, a fair number are investigated, and in some cases, disciplined for professional misconduct. Drawing upon unique data provided by the State Bar of California, this article examines the entire population of lawyers admitted to practice in California from 1990 to 2024 to explore who gets investigated and disciplined, and why. Relying on these same factors, however, would exclude many more lawyers who never run afoul of the professional rules. We argue that the existing, largely reactive regulatory framework could benefit from a more proactive, evidence-based approach. A more promising approach, we posit, is for regulators to identify lawyers statistically at risk of investigation and discipline, providing them with training and resources to avoid the most common forms of attorney misconduct.

Sapna Kumar & Yinuo Nolan Zhu

Abstract:
Concerned about a proliferation of bad patents that harmed innovation, Congress made it easier for people to challenge patent validity by creating an administrative procedure known as inter partes review (IPR). Faster and cheaper than litigating in federal court, IPRs surged in popularity between 2012 and 2025. This has emboldened the current Director to create even more reasons to refuse IPR institution, and has led to him denying hundreds of IPR petitions without explaining the reason why -- a process known as summary denials. This Article argues that the Patent Office has violated the APA by failing to utilize notice-and-comment rulemaking for making substantive changes to IPRs and by failing to provide explanations for its decisions made through informal adjudication. It further maintains that the Federal Circuit’s broad construal of both § 701 and § 314 is in tension with the Supreme Court’s recent administrative law decisions, which counterbalance strong Presidential authority over agencies with heightened judicial oversight. This Article argues that a narrower interpretation of these provisions is the only way to avoid a nondelegation doctrine violation under the U.S. Constitution.

Adoption as Authorship
Christopher Newman
George Washington Journal of Law & Technology, forthcoming

Abstract:
The U.S. Copyright Office treats expression generated by AI as categorically unprotectable, even when a human directs the process and incorporates the output into a work. This Article argues that the Office's position rests on a mistaken model of authorship, in which the author must personally generate each element of fixed expression or at least transcribe a precise mental conception formed in advance. Neither model describes how authors actually work. Creation proceeds by trial and error. Authors generate expressive variations, often through processes they do not control, and settle on results that fulfill an intent that may itself change along the way. Photographers shooting in burst mode, Ellsworth Kelly’s randomly dropped paper fragments, and Judge Frank’s “clap of thunder” in Alfred Bell & Co. v. Catalda all show that copyright already recognizes authorship of expression the author did not deliberately generate. The Article contends that the irreducible act of authorship is adoption, meaning the choice to treat a set of sensory signals as the embodiment of one's expressive intent. The joint authorship cases support this account. They locate authorship in decision-making authority over what the work will contain, not in the generation of content. The adoption theory does not license appropriating preexisting material, because originality doctrine separately bars claims to the commons or to others' expression. On this reading, originality works like the Lockean limits on appropriation. AI output is abundant and takes nothing from the commons, so there is no principled reason to deny protection to a human author who adopts it as her own expression.

Cameron Ellis, Johannes Gerd Jaspersen & Valentin Luz
University of Iowa Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:

We document multiple mechanisms consistent with strategic manipulation, including leveraging institutional knowledge and exploiting publicly observable examiner workloads. We develop a simple model of manipulation investments that explains which firms are most likely to game the patent lottery and show empirical support for its predictions. Our findings challenge the fairness of the patent lottery. This can have significant welfare implications, both in terms of efficiency -- generating as much innovation as possible -- and in terms of equity. We further highlight the economic significance of law firms, which, despite their prevalence, have received relatively little empirical attention. Lastly, we call into question empirical designs that rely on examiner randomization for causal identification.

New molecular and historical evidence on ancient Egyptian embalming
Tim Berger et al.
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 10 November 2026

Abstract:
Mumia vera aegyptiaca was a mummy-derived medicinal substance widely used in medieval and early modern medicine, yet its material composition and biological activity remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate Egyptological and pharmaceutical-historical analysis of 41 textual sources with LC–MS/MS-based metabolomics, molecular networking, machine-learning-assisted annotation, and bioactivity testing to investigate ancient Egyptian embalming materials and historical Mumia vera samples. We analyzed 24 objects from university and pharmacy museum collections, including historical Mumia vera products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. Comparative metabolomics revealed substantial heterogeneity among materials labeled as Mumia vera, but also recurrent molecular signatures consistent with aged conifer resins, including oxidized abietane-type diterpenoids. Several samples contained Aloe-associated metabolites, including aloeresin A/D- and aloin-related compounds. These data reveal Aloe-associated metabolites in ancient Egyptian embalming-related materials and support the presence of Aloe spp.-derived exudates in selected samples. The convergence of molecular and textual evidence further raises the possibility that a previously unresolved Egyptian term from the 2nd millennium BC may refer to Aloe sp. or an Aloe-derived product. Comparative metabolomics also linked an inconspicuous powder sample to a specific mummified head, although their curatorial association had not been securely documented. Finally, a historical Mumia vera aegyptiaca extract modestly protected MDCK cells from influenza virus-induced cytopathic effects, whereas the isolated major compound 7-oxodehydroabietic acid was inactive on its own. item.title: Generational Estimates — Demographics and growing up
item.description:
Why has low fertility become a polarized issue?
John Iceland
Theory and Society, December 2026

Abstract:
Most countries today have below-replacement fertility and the global population is projected to decline before the century’s end. Potential consequences include fiscal challenges of an aging population, slower economic growth, and weakened kinship networks. Yet the policy response of demographers has been relatively muted compared to their more active role in promoting population control during periods of rapid growth. While substantive considerations help explain disagreement over whether low fertility is a problem, this paper examines how competing moral frameworks -- rooted in Social Justice and Social Order -- may also shape public and academic responses to low fertility. I begin with a historical comparison between the politics of population growth and today’s debate about population decline and develop a framework linking moral orientations to different understandings of demographic change and appropriate policy responses. I then use large language models to analyze the moral framing of fertility research published in eight leading demographic journals from 1947 to 2025. While most article abstracts contained neither moral frame, among those that did, 83% employed a Social Justice frame and 17% a Social Order frame, with Social Justice framing becoming increasingly prominent over time. I conclude by arguing that the predominance of Social Justice orientations may contribute to the muted response to low fertility, given that efforts to increase fertility align more closely with Social Order concerns, and that recognizing the moral dimensions of demographic debates can facilitate more constructive engagement.

When success stops producing more descendants: Behavioral return, fitness return, and the parity-specific decoupling behind below-replacement fertility
Albina Gallyamova & Dmitry Grigoryev
Evolutionary Behavioral Sciences, forthcoming

Abstract:
Across many posttransitional societies, fertility has fallen below replacement even while reported family-size ideals often remain near or above two children. Because stated ideals are imperfect indicators of reproductive preferences and are declining in some populations, this pattern is not universal; the present framework addresses settings in which reported aspirations continue to exceed achieved fertility. We connect this demographic issue to a longstanding problem in human sociobiology: Why success in socially valued domains no longer maps reliably onto reproductive and descendant success. We distinguish fitness return on investment (fROI), the long-horizon conversion of a practice into descendant output and lineage persistence, from behavioral return on investment (bROI), the behavior-regulating payoff structure that governs whether a practice is adopted, maintained, delayed, or abandoned in a given social ecology. We argue that posttransitional environments can produce partial, sex-specific, and parity-specific decoupling between these returns: Practices that yield security, status, risk reduction, or social approval may remain behaviorally advantageous while delaying or suppressing reproduction. The reproductive sequence includes a context-dependent preparity partnership gate that can constrain entry into parenthood. The four principal pathways -- preparation, postponement, support, and quality intensification -- alter the probabilities of transitions from 0 → 1, 1 → 2, and 2 → 3+ children, with preparation also shaping access to the gate itself. Because information about proximate returns is visible and culturally transmissible, whereas descendant consequences are delayed, high-bROI practices can persist after their coupling to long-run fROI has weakened. This framework explains how a culturally salient family-size ideal can coexist with a parity structure that does not sustain replacement and yields testable propositions for evolutionary demography, human behavioral ecology, and cultural evolution.

Changes in American adolescents’ outdoor time over two decades
Ewa Jarosz, Vidar Ulset & Vegard Skirbekk
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 3 November 2026

Abstract:
Spending time outdoors provides opportunities for physical activity, exposure to natural light, and social contact. Although young people’s time use has changed substantially in recent decades, little is known about long-term trends in adolescents’ outdoor engagement. This question is especially important because adolescence is a period of major life transitions and the development of lasting behavioral habits. This study examines 20-y trends in time spent outdoors among American adolescents using time-diary data from 14,235 individuals aged 15 to 19 in the 2003-2023 American Time Use Survey, a nationally representative survey of the US population. We describe trends in outdoor exposure and examine associations between outdoor time and leisure behaviors, including computer use for leisure, indoor physical activity, and time spent with friends. We find that outdoor engagement among boys has declined sharply, erasing a long-standing male advantage and causing boys’ participation levels to converge with girls’ at similarly low rates. Greater time spent in computer-based leisure was associated with less outdoor time, particularly among boys, whereas time spent with friends was positively associated with outdoor engagement for both sexes. Indoor physical activity did not change over the observation period and did not offset declines in outdoor time. These findings suggest that broader changes in leisure activities may be reshaping how young people engage with outdoor environments. Further research is needed to better understand the factors underlying these trends and their potential long-term implications.

Genetic Influences on Human Capital Development
Philip Monagan
University of Chicago Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
This paper investigates how genes and household investment choices jointly shape skills and educational attainment during adolescence. Using data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, I exploit random genetic variation between siblings to identify a causal schooling effect of 0.47 years per standard deviation of a genetic score for educational attainment, compared with 0.66 years without family fixed effects. Controlling for parental education and household income attenuates the estimate to 0.42 years, suggesting these controls alone absorb much of the confounding induced by parents passing down both genes and other advantages. Reduced-form estimates cannot separate direct genetic effects from parental responses, while within-family investment regressions cannot detect parental investments shared by both siblings. Sibling spillovers also contaminate the pooled-within-family gap, and interaction terms in outcome regressions conflate skill technology with parental choices. I therefore estimate a structural model of skill production and parental investment using the simulated method of moments. I find a direct genetic effect on cognitive skill, little gene-investment complementarity, and evidence that parents reinforce sibling differences by reducing leisure and reallocating investment time toward the higher-score sibling. Finally, I use the model to evaluate policy interventions while accounting for endogenous household responses.

Changing contributions of emotion and reward information to learning through adolescence
Camille Phaneuf-Hadd, Elizabeth Phelps & Leah Somerville
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 20 October 2026

Abstract:
From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8 to 22 y completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hampered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially hindered by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

item.title: Learning by the Numbers — Educating the next generation
item.description:
The Unintended Consequences of Academic Leniency
Brooks Bowden, Viviana Rodriguez & Zach Weingarten
American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, November 2026, Pages 130-159

Abstract:
Education is widely recognized as the primary driver of human capital accumulation. However, policies designed to promote educational attainment often overlook students' endogenous responses. This paper provides empirical evidence of the causal impact of relaxed academic standards on student effort and achievement. We find that academic leniency results in mechanical GPA increases, but significant reductions in effort among lower ability students based on lower attendance and lower numerical grades. These heterogeneous effects compound and exacerbate gaps in engagement and achievement throughout high school, ultimately worsening deficits in human capital accumulation as measured by ACT scores.

What Drives Censorship on College Campuses?
Peter Arcidiacono, Cory Dowd & Matthew Lilley
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
There has been widespread concern about self-censorship on university campuses, and especially that conservative voices are being stifled. Using survey data from a private elite college, we show that self-censorship is not simply about being conservative: it is students with the most moderate views who self-censor the most. This pattern is associated with confidence and salience -- students who are more confident in their views or who see an issue as especially important tend to hold more extreme views and to self-censor less. At the same time, conservatives self-censor at higher rates than liberals, and the same individual is more likely to self-censor on the views where they are relatively more conservative than on those where they are relatively more liberal; conservatives are also far more likely than liberals to cite concerns about social exclusion as a reason for self-censoring, and report self-censoring less outside the university community. Groups perceived as marginalized self-censor less than majority groups, and especially so on issues salient to them (e.g., Black students on BLM).

A Defense of Affirmative Action for Conservatives
Daniel Jacobson
Philosophy & Public Affairs, forthcoming

Abstract:
The suggestion that academia should promote political diversity, implying as it does that the status quo is severely deficient, is commonly rejected on the grounds that to do so would require “affirmative action for conservatives.” That conclusion is typically treated as a reductio ad absurdum even by those who support conventional race- and sex-based affirmative action. Nevertheless, this paper defends affirmative action for conservatives on both negative and positive grounds. It argues that since conservatives are discriminated against throughout academia, policies that benefit them in admissions and hiring would not be unjust to those who bear its burden. And it argues that the advantages of increased political diversity would accrue not just to those with heterodox opinions but would improve the intellectual atmosphere of academia at large. Hence, conservative affirmative action promotes the traditional academic mission and its norms of meritocracy, academic freedom, and the pursuit of knowledge; and it is not unjust to those with orthodox political views.

College Success: Understanding the Roles of Financial Aid, Loans, Preparation, and Incentives
Douglas Harris, Christopher Taber & Yu (Alan) Yang
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
Over the past four decades, the earnings gap between college graduates and non-graduates has widened substantially, prompting interest in policies aimed at promoting higher education among low-income students. A key challenge for these policies is the high college dropout rate. This paper develops a dynamic model of college enrollment and completion with rich individual heterogeneity to assess how various factors influence college attendance, dropout, and graduation. We estimate the model using data from longitudinal surveys, results of quasi-experimental studies on grant aid, and large-scale randomized controlled trials. We use the model to simulate the effects of tuition subsidies, college loans, financial incentives, and increased pre-college skills on attendance and completion. We find moderate effects of most unconditional financial policies on attendance, with small effects on completion conditional on attendance. By contrast, some merit-based incentives, such as forgiving student loans upon receipt of a bachelor’s degree, have substantial effects. However, this type of policy and other financial subsidies accrue even more than the others to students from relatively wealthy backgrounds. Overall, it appears infeasible to design a financial aid policy that is simultaneously effective in raising attainment and fiscally progressive. By comparison, we find that the greatest potential for increasing attainment could come from better preparing students for college.

Gary King & Steven Worthington
Harvard Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
We show that AI-generated article reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts and judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors. We then discuss how this result may inform journal policy choices, with concerning downsides as well as potential paths to increase publication speed and quality; reduce adversarial interactions; improve the experience of editors, reviewers, authors, and readers; and advance science.

Yerin Yoon
Education Finance and Policy, forthcoming

Abstract:
Connecticut expanded interdistrict magnet schools (IMS) intending to reduce racial and socioeconomic segregation across districts, yet the potential unintended effects on student composition in nearby schools remains unclear. Leveraging the staggered rollout of IMS openings, this study finds that IMS openings reduce enrollment by about 5 percent in nearby private K8 and traditional public high schools (TPHS). In private K8, the share of White students declines by 3.5 percent, reducing White exposure for remaining Black and Hispanic students, with effects driven by Catholic schools. In TPHS, the share of students eligible for free or reduced-price lunch increases by 18 percent, suggesting that higher-income students are more likely to exit, with larger effects in a region under court-ordered desegregation. These findings suggest that policies designed to reduce segregation across districts may have unintended socioeconomic and racial compositional consequences for the students left behind in nearby schools.

Yasemin Copur-Gencturk, Ian Thacker & Joseph Cimpian
Educational Researcher, forthcoming

Abstract:

We randomly assigned 963 teachers to provide feedback either “as you normally would” (control) or to emphasize “your high standards and that the student has the potential to meet them” (treatment). Treatment teachers gave more detailed feedback on students’ strengths, weaknesses, strategies, effort, and math ability, with less positive ability-related feedback offered to girls and lower effort demanded from White male students. This study is the first to demonstrate that prompting high expectation feedback changes the substance of teacher comments. Brooks Bowden, Viviana Rodriguez & Zach Weingarten
American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, November 2026, Pages 130-159

Abstract:

Abstract:
