item.description:
The Impact of the Great Recession on Mortality: A Dynamic Factor Analysis
Amy Finkelstein, Matthew Notowidigdo & Enzo Profili
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
We use a dynamic factor time series model to estimate the national mortality impact of the Great Recession. In aggregate, the Great Recession reduced the average annual, age-adjusted mortality rate by about 2 percent, with effects persisting for at least a decade. In a calibrated model of the welfare effects of the estimated impacts of the Great Recession on consumption and mortality, we find that the welfare gain from the estimated mortality decline is quantitatively significant relative to the welfare loss from the estimated consumption decline. The estimated mortality decline is also quantitatively close to prior mortality estimates using cross-sectional variation in the severity of the Great Recession, implying limited general equilibrium effects of the Great Recession on mortality. More broadly, our findings suggest that prior evidence from local labor markets that recessions are good for health can be extrapolated to the likely mortality consequences of nationwide recessions.

Science or advocacy? The global rise of policy claims and calls to action in population health research (1990-2024)
David Bann et al.
American Journal of Epidemiology, November 2026, Pages 2927-2936

Abstract:
Should original research articles routinely contain prominent policy claims or broad calls to action? Growing emphasis on research impact might be welcome yet have unintended consequences (eg, incentivizing overextrapolation and undermining the perceived objectivity of scientists). We examined 45 807 abstracts from 10 leading Epidemiology and Public Health journals (1990-2024). Using a large language model with human validation, we classified policy claims and mapped trends. Claims markedly increased from 17.6% to 35.8%, with wide variation across countries and journals (>60% vs <4%). Keywords linked to higher claim rates differed by topic and time: some corresponded to topics with clear causal evidence of harm as well as topics with notable advocacy. Claims were most common in qualitative or cross-sectional studies, and less common in cohort, quasi-experimental, or experimental studies. We argue that these patterns reflect a research culture increasingly oriented toward claiming policy relevance -- and incentives that encourage attaching claims to single studies. Our findings raise questions about how scientists and journals balance evidence, advocacy, and scientific credibility. Ensuring that policy claims and calls to action remain commensurate with evidence will be central to building trust as policy impact continues to be incentivized.

Risk Assessment of an Illegal Laboratory in Reedley, California, Using Geospatial Analysis of Open-Source Epidemic Intelligence Data
Atalay Goshu Muluneh et al.
Risk Analysis, November 2026

Abstract:
An illegal laboratory discovered in Reedley, California, in December 2022 was in a warehouse, operating without a license, handling about a thousand transgenic mice, chemicals, and possibly over 20 pathogens, including vials labeled Ebola, which were never tested but destroyed. This study aimed to estimate epidemic signals around the Reedley illegal laboratory using open-source epidemic intelligence data. We utilized data from EPIWATCH, from October 2021 to October 2023, a year prior to and a year after the establishment of the illegal laboratory. The spatial pattern of outbreak signals was analyzed using hotspot analysis, and the distances of outbreak signals from the laboratory were measured. In California, an upward trend in outbreak signals of pathogens associated with the laboratory was noted in December 2022, April 2023, and August 2023. In the hotspot analysis, California and eight other states in the United States (US) were identified as hotspots. Narrative evidence revealed the presence of a sick employee working in the laboratory, whose child also became ill. Changes in disease patterns reported in California or the US in the year following the establishment of the illegal laboratory may or may not be linked to the illegal laboratory. A subsequent illegal lab linked to Reedley was identified in Las Vegas in 2026, highlighting the ongoing threat to biosecurity. EPIWATCH geospatial and temporal analysis can enhance the public health risk assessment of threats associated with illegal laboratories, especially when there is no available testing or reporting.

Sanchita Chakrovorty & Travis Smith

Abstract:
Population health is a central input into social welfare, but health itself is complex and multidimensional. Mapping multiple dimensions of health into a single population health index may require strong assumptions about how to aggregate and weight across dimensions. This study adopts a novel nonparametric approach to rank individual health as a function of seven biomarkers associated with major domains of physiological health: body mass index (BMI), glycohemoglobin (HbA1c), total cholesterol, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and white blood cell (WBC). This approach avoids arbitrary weighting while requiring only monotonicity and quasi-concavity. Using NHANES data from 1988 to 2018, we document a significant deterioration in the U.S. health distribution, with declines concentrated in the lower tail. Counterfactual decompositions show that one-third of the negative shift can be attributed to an aging, more racially and ethnically diverse population, leaving a remaining portion unexplained by observed factors. The findings highlight the value of distribution-sensitive multidimensional health measures for monitoring health inequality and targeting preventive care.

NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:

Leveraging state-level variation in the timing of P-EBT disbursements using a stacked difference-in-differences identification strategy with NielsenIQ Consumer Panel data, we find that P-EBT disbursement was associated with a 16-percent increase in weekly spending on sugary items among SNAP-eligible households with school-aged children. Notably, this increase exceeded the percentage increase in overall food spending for this group, suggesting that SNAP-eligible households with school-aged children allocated a disproportionately large share of their P-EBT-driven purchases toward sugary items relative to their pre-period baseline. We do not detect changes among households unlikely to have received P-EBT benefits or in placebo disbursement years.

Matthew Brown
Health Economics, November 2026, Pages 1764-1791

Abstract:
A near majority of states have now passed recreational marijuana laws (RMLs), but their impact on labor market behavior remains unclear. This study provides new causal evidence on the relationship between RMLs and workplace absence. Next, I show that retail market access leads to a 14% increase in the incidence of prior-week workplace absence. Supplemental analyses of health outcomes suggest that part of the effect may be driven by increases in self-reported mental health problems following the opening of recreational dispensaries. These findings suggest that marijuana legalization may affect labor market outcomes along margins not typically captured by employment status alone.

Amy Finkelstein, Matthew Notowidigdo & Charlie Rafkin
NBER Working Paper, November 2026

Abstract:
We analyze the food stamp program both as a potential investment in children’s health capital and as a redistributive tool by studying the 1979 reform that made food stamps free. We leverage geographic variation in exposure to the reform, which raised the program’s food subsidy from 65% to 100%. This raised enrollment by 1.85 percentage points (standard error = 0.15), or about 25%, with new enrollees substantially poorer than existing participants. From an investment perspective, we do not find evidence of improvement in infant health, and 95% confidence intervals rule out gains in birth weight from enrolling in food stamps exceeding 2%. From a redistribution perspective, the enrollment response implies that the average recipient of free food stamps acts as if they value them at 59 cents per dollar, with nonparametric bounds of 42–77 cents. Despite this substantial dissipation in transfer value relative to a frictionless cash transfer, under standard redistributive preferences the free food stamp program increases social welfare because of its targeting to very low-income households. The move to free stamps from a partially subsidized program improved targeting on social value but worsened targeting on private value.

Brian Curran & Michael McKelligott
University of Chicago Working Paper, November 2026

Abstract:

While existing literature has explored the role of public health initiatives in explaining this decline from the latter of these types, this paper focuses on the contribution of innovations in and provision of hygienic technologies and their role in eradication of the former. Specifically, we investigate the health impact of the rapid adoption and utilization of bathhouses in urban working-class neighborhoods following the technological advancement of what we recognize today as the modern-day shower. By exploiting differential timing of bathhouse openings beginning around 1890 and utilizing city-level mortality data for U.S. urban areas, we estimate the mortality effects of these facilities introduced prior to the widespread adoption of modern household sanitation infrastructure and the germ theory of disease. This paper highlights the role that hygienic infrastructure and behavior may have played in improving public health during that era, shedding light on mechanisms policy makers can utilize when designing interventions aimed at encouraging behavioral take-up today.

item.title: Incoming and Outgoing — Effects of immigration and globalization
item.description:
Economic models and policy goals in evaluating US H-1B visa fees
David Green & Stephen Tino
Labour Economics, forthcoming

Abstract:
Recent debate over the US $100,000 H-1B visa fee has focused on measuring the wage gap between H-1B workers and comparable native-born workers. We argue that this gap, whatever its size, cannot by itself tell us what the fee would do or whether it is good policy. To answer the first question, we start from economic theory rather than measurement issues in the data. Using a search-and-bargaining model in which H-1B workers cannot change employers, we show that the gap mixes markdowns with the sorting of H-1B workers into less productive firms. We also show that the fee acts as a tax on the output of H-1B matches, and that the workers themselves bear part of it. Whether the fee raises or lowers welfare depends on the elasticity of labour demand, how much bargaining power H-1B workers have, and how congested the labour market is. To answer the second question, we need to be explicit about the policy goal. Because the H-1B system is already a second-best setting, efficiency cannot be separated from justice. Any policy in this setting creates winners and losers, so choosing one means taking a position on justice, even when the case for it is made on efficiency grounds alone. Neutral policy advice should therefore also measure outcomes that matter under non-welfarist conceptions of justice, such as how firms treat visa holders and how the immigration process shapes newcomers' views of the society they join.

The Labor Market Impact of Temporary High-Skill Immigration Programs
George Borjas
NBER Working Paper, November 2026

Abstract:

What Do “Most People” Believe? Race, Gender, and the Generalized Other
Natasha Quadlin et al.
American Sociological Review, forthcoming

Abstract:
When people form beliefs in social life, they often calibrate their own thinking against what they anticipate “most people” think. Although prior research demonstrates the importance of these inferences, scholars have yet to examine who is best proxied by “most people.” Given persistent inequalities in U.S. society that advantage White men, as well as theories of cultural hegemony, we hypothesize that “most people’s” imagined beliefs are closely proxied by those of White men. We test these ideas using an original survey experiment conducted with a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults (N = 2,089) in which we adapt 64 core items from the General Social Survey. Respondents were randomly assigned to answer these questions either from the perspective of most people, or from the perspective of designated race-gender groups. Contrary to our hypothesis, we find strong and consistent evidence that White men are not seen as standard-bearers for most social issues. Instead, perceptions of what most people believe are highly aligned with the imagined beliefs of White women. Importantly, this pattern emerges not because White women are seen as influential, but because White women are perceived as less extreme than other groups. We also observe variation across respondents, such that respondents tend to center their own race-gender group in conceptualizing most people’s beliefs (with White women typically close behind).

The Greater Female Vulnerability Hypothesis: Women’s traits are designed to elicit care
Tania Reynolds
Behavioral and Brain Sciences, forthcoming

Abstract:
Because mothers were more critical to offspring survival than fathers, women faced pressures to ensure their survival. If social partners could provide food and aid, ancestral women faced selective pressures to recruit support by communicating need. Compared to men, women 1.) are more concerned about social acceptance, 2.) perceive themselves as more vulnerable, 3.) more readily communicate suffering, 4.) more effectively elicit sympathy, 5.) and more often suffer from psychopathologies communicating desperation. Female psychopathology has worsened despite increased resources and opportunities, suggesting it does not entirely reflect absolute deprivation, but rather, is a competitive adaptation activated by heightened social competition.

Constructing Sexual Harassment: How Gender, Race, and Sector Patterned #MeToo Media Coverage
Chloe Grace Hart & Xuan Nguyen
Social Currents, forthcoming

Abstract:
The #MeToo movement was a period of unprecedented media attention to sexual harassment, reshaping public perception and spurring institutional reforms. However, scholars and activists have observed that media coverage seemed to disproportionately feature White, economically privileged women. We provide a quantitative analysis of demographic patterns in #MeToo media coverage by systematically coding articles mentioning sexual harassment from CNN and The New York Times during the movement’s peak (October 2017 to January 2018; N = 1,560), with additional data from Fox News through mid-November 2017 (N = 324). We find that White women indeed dominated coverage as targets (78% of identifiable cases) and White men as perpetrators (89% of identifiable cases). Men accounted for only 4% of targets, far below their representation in prevalence surveys. Coverage concentrated in high-profile sectors -- motion pictures, broadcasting, and politics -- while low-wage sectors remained nearly invisible. These patterns were consistent across ideologically distinct outlets (though Fox News limited coverage of cases involving conservative figures). Thus, despite its transformative potential, #MeToo media coverage reproduced existing hierarchies of credibility, centering privileged White women while marginalizing racial minorities, men, and low-wage workers. These patterns have implications for public understanding of sexual harassment, including whose experiences are deemed credible.

The Development of Gender Stereotypes About Service
Sophie Arnold, Katharina Block & Andrei Cimpian
Developmental Science, January 2027

Abstract:
At work and at home, women perform more service than men, often at a personal cost. We investigated a psychological factor that may contribute to this disparity: an early-emerging descriptive gender stereotype that associates service with girls. We compared 5- to 8-year-old children's (N = 192) and adults’ (N = 192) expectations about whether girls or boys would help across three types of scenarios: (a) interpersonal helping (which benefited a specific individual), (b) non-costly service (which benefited a collective at no cost to the helper), and (c) costly service (which benefited a collective at a cost to the helper). Participants associated girls more than boys with costly service specifically. This association was especially noticeable among boys and men, who showed neutral expectations about interpersonal helping and non-costly service but expected girls (vs. boys) to perform costly service. Girls and women showed a broader tendency to expect girls (vs. boys) to help across contexts. Separately, we also measured more general communality stereotypes (i.e., beliefs that girls are more other-oriented than boys). These stereotypes predicted expectations about costly service but did not fully account for them: The association between girls and costly service persisted even after adjusting for individual differences in these stereotypes. These findings suggest that gendered expectations are strongest when helping demands personal sacrifice for a group or institution. These intensified expectations are already in place by ages 5 to 8, potentially representing one pathway through which gender disparities in service behavior develop over time.

Jeanne Bovet et al.
Proceedings of the Royal Society: Biological Sciences, November 2026

Abstract:

In this study, we show that these transformations began much earlier and reflect long-term cultural evolution in aesthetic preferences. Using a novel dataset of 606 painted women from European elite portraits (1650–1950) and independent perceptual ratings from over 1500 participants, we reconstruct historical changes in women's perceived waist-to-hip ratio (WHR), a well-documented cue of youth and reproductive potential. We find a significant and robust increase in WHR over time, independent of perceived age and weight, suggesting a shift away from curvaceous silhouettes towards more androgynous representations. Perceived facial age also increased, and overall body attractiveness ratings decreased, consistent with a declining emphasis on youthfulness and reproductive cues. These findings suggest a gradual reconfiguration of aesthetic values in the representation of women, and these trends parallel known demographic and economic transitions in early modern Europe, such as delayed reproduction and rising investment in education, although exploratory analyses linking perceived WHR directly to historical fertility rates did not show associations independent of the passage of time itself. Our findings illustrate how visual artefacts can serve as ‘cognitive fossils,’ capturing deep historical shifts in psychological preferences and reproductive strategies.

Tessa Charlesworth, Meriel Doyle & Mahzarin Banaji
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 10 November 2026

Abstract:
Between 2007 and 2020, implicit and explicit intergroup attitudes declined in bias steadily and were forecasted to continue toward attitude neutrality. But, since 2020, 5 y of new data (2021–2025) from 2.8 million U.S. respondents reveal that past trends have stalled or, in some cases, even reversed. The largest reversals in bias emerged for sexuality, transgender, race, and skin-tone bias which increased by 12 to 22% on implicit measures and by 24% to more than tripling on explicit measures. Age, disability, and body weight bias also increased, but at relatively slower rates. Breakpoint analyses showed that implicit attitudes were early indicators of change, reversing trend ~1 y earlier than explicit reports. For most topics, reversals were widespread across demographic groups and even extended to an international sample of 274,884 non-U.S. respondents. However, younger respondents (<20-y-old) -- who had previously shown the largest decreases in bias -- now showed the largest increases in bias; these trends also interacted with politics and gender (e.g., young conservative men were the most likely to increase). Exploratory analyses ruled out various single-cause explanations. Instead, we suggest that the best explanation is that 2020–2021 marked a turning point in the sociopolitical climate, whereby co-occurring existential threats from the COVID-19 pandemic, amplified economic insecurity, political sectarianism, and online toxicity prompted increases in intergroup bias. These data underscore how large populations of individual-level attitudes are continually shaped and altered by macro, societal-level events.

Luyin Zhang & Sam Trejo
Demography, forthcoming

Abstract:

Consequently, the empirical distributions and measurement properties of GSPs remain underexplored. Utilizing a unique survey question on respondents’ self-reported ancestral countries, we observe that -- although a person's self-reported ancestry is associated with their GSPs -- there exists considerable variation in GSPs among individuals with the same self-reported ancestry. In addition, among respondents who self-report ancestry from the Americas or from sub-Saharan Africa, GSPs are robustly associated with skin tone and racial classification, suggesting that such measures index individual characteristics that are racialized in contemporary American society. We close by discussing how GSPs could inform demographic research on the evolving racial, ethnic, and ancestral diversity of the United States.

item.title: Thousands of Years — Ancient humans
item.description:
The Nighthawk Bison Jump: New Evidence for Recurrent Late Holocene Bison Jumping in the Southern Plains
August Costa et al.
American Antiquity, forthcoming

Abstract:
Large-scale communal bison hunting via jumping is a renowned tactic best known from the northern Plains. In contrast, evidence for jumps in the southern Plains is sparse and controversial. The paucity of bison jumps in the southern Plains has been attributed by some to a lack of suitable precipices. Yet the eastern Caprock Escarpment of the Llano Estacado (in the Southern High Plains) presents numerous scarps suitable for bison jumping. Recent investigations at the Nighthawk site in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle have revealed an exceptional record of at least seven discrete kill events spanning 3,000 years from the Late Archaic to Protohistoric periods. We present the results of 27 direct radiocarbon measurements on bone collagen and charcoal, reconstruct site formation processes, and describe the skeletal composition of each kill and lithic evidence from this long-term hunting facility. These new data challenge many long-held assumptions about the nature of bison jump hunting techniques in time and space.

Evidence for late Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus in mainland East Asia
Wei Liao et al.
Nature, forthcoming

Abstract:
Hominin fossils and genetic evidence indicate that several hominin populations occupied East and Southeast Asia during the Middle and Late Pleistocene epoch. Homo erectus fossils remain scarce in southern China and mainland Southeast Asia. Here we report nine newly discovered late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves at the Chongzuo study area, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, southern China, dated to around 324–184 thousand years ago. Palaeoproteomics reveals the presence of an endogenous dental proteome in all five hominin teeth studied molecularly. Four teeth contain a derived H. erectus substitution in ameloblastin that to date has been observed only in older Middle Pleistocene H. erectus specimens from China. The proteomes of these four teeth differ from the previous H. erectus proteomes from China at another ameloblastin position, suggesting that these specimens represent a previously unsampled H. erectus population. Morphometric and geometric morphometric methods support an attribution of these teeth to H. erectus, as well as four additional teeth. This fills a gap in the geographical and chronological distribution of H. erectus in East Asia. The fifth tooth studied proteomically, PA1796, is morphologically distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) and modern humans (Homo sapiens), and does not contain the H. erectus-derived amino acid sequence. The late survival of H. erectus on mainland East Asia suggests that at least two hominin lineages, H. erectus and Homo longi (Denisovans), possibly represented by PA1796, were present in the region towards the end of the Middle Pleistocene, with the first documented occurrence of H. sapiens not much later.

A Mixed Coastal–Terrestrial Model of Adaptation in ISEA Reflecting on the Two Southern Routes of Early Modern Human Migration
Hendri Kaharudin, Sue O’Connor & Shimona Kealy
Journal of Archaeological Research, December 2026, Pages 757-819

Abstract:
This study revisits models of early modern human–coastal adaptation in Island Southeast Asia, a region central to understanding two major dispersal events: the initial Out of Africa movement towards southern Asia and the subsequent colonisation of Sahul via Wallacea. We distinguish episodic or opportunistic pre-Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) sea crossings from sustained, year-round coastal subsistence, which appears to have intensified only after the LGM. Focusing on archaeological evidence from the Lesser Sunda Islands, we propose an alternative model that somewhat reconciles both the traditional view of systematic marine exploitation emerging in the Mid- to Late Holocene and the revisionist claims of intensive coastal use as early as 160,000 years ago. Instead, our findings suggest a more gradual trajectory of adaptation following the LGM, structured into four phases: early occupation (50–23 ka) characterised by a focus on terrestrial subsistence supplemented with aquatic resources; post-LGM adaptation (22–16 ka) marked by increasing coastal resource use; a peak maritime phase during rapid sea-level rise (15–8 ka); and Mid- to Late Holocene settlement (7 ka–present) when terrestrial and marine resources became more integrated. Isotopic data and faunal assemblages reflect flexible, context-dependent subsistence strategies across Wallacea. The northern corridor likely supported denser populations and functioned as a key migration hub, while the southern route became more viable post-LGM due to expanding intertidal zones. This model reframes coastal resources not as a singular driving force but as complementary elements in a dynamic, environmentally mediated adaptive process during early modern human migration through Southeast Asia.

The deep Palaeolithic Roots of the South-west Asian Neolithic
Trevor Watkins
Proceedings of the Prehistoric Society, forthcoming

Abstract:
This paper sets out to see an aspect of the Neolithic of south-west Asia in the context of its cultural evolutionary history: essential components of the architecture of Neolithic communities -- hearth and home, and intramural burial -- were present as architectural components of social life tens and hundreds of thousands of years before they were accommodated within Neolithic houses. There are two bases that underpin the paper. One is the general view of cultural evolution and cultural niche construction theory that has emerged over recent decades, emphasising human ultra-sociality and capacity for altruism and cooperation; the other is the understanding of architecture as more than built structures, encompassing objects in, on and around buildings, associated meanings and values, and behaviours. We may trace the development of the architecture of social life as it fostered the intensity of social relations, effectively the roots of Neolithic social life. The process begins at least three quarters of a million years ago with the control of fire, cooking, and eating together around the hearth. The evolution of the human cultural niche continues with the emergence around half a million years ago of the idea of the base camp. That is followed about one hundred thousand years ago by the burying of the body of a member of the group below the base camp floor, binding place and belonging into social memory. The Epipalaeolithic–Neolithic transformation represents a quickening of the pace of cultural cumulation in the specific environment of the hilly flanks of the Fertile Crescent in south-west Asia, with the extension of the group’s stay for at least a season, and the growth in size of the group. The first large, co-resident communities designed and built permanent settlements, houses with hearths, communal buildings, and ritualised intramural burials, forming a new and meaningful architecture of social life embedded in social memory.

A Rare Corner-Tang Knife and Obsidian Acquisition in the Cypress Hills: Long-Distance Interaction Networks on the Northern Plains
Kyle Robert Belanger et al.
American Antiquity, forthcoming

Abstract:
The movement of peoples, goods, and ideas across the North American Great Plains may be inferred by sourcing raw materials and documenting the spatiotemporal distribution of artifact types. One such form of artifact is the corner-tang knife, a notched biface with a tang opposite the cutting edge. Based on more than a century of investigations, corner-tang knives are understood to have originated in central Texas, from where the technology quickly spread. However, few specimens derive from dated, undisturbed contexts from either the United States or Canada. Here, we report on a corner-tang knife from the Middle to Late prehistoric site of DjOn-8 (∼3600–250 BP) in the Cypress Hills, Alberta (Canada) along with its archaeological context and obsidian sourcing results. The knife in question is a diagonal variant manufactured from local chalcedony. Use-wear analysis indicates that it was hafted and used for cutting, whereas protein antigen precipitates suggest that the knife was used to process large ungulates. Obsidian artifacts recovered from DjOn-8 are sourced to Bear Gulch (Idaho) and Obsidian Cliff (Wyoming), more than 500 km away. Our findings shed light on the nature and complexity of trade and interaction networks across the Great Plains and underscore the potential for consulting archaeologists to contribute meaningfully to archaeological discourse.

item.title: Going Live — Market research
item.description:
Strategic information asceticism: Denying self to deny others
John Allenbach & Richard Zeckhauser
Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, October 2026, Pages 183-209

Abstract:
This paper introduces strategic information asceticism. A decision maker deliberately forgoes acquiring valuable information because possessing it may let others obtain it -- through direct monitoring, leaks, or compulsory disclosure -- and then act against her, say by entering her market. To preempt such competitive responses, Apple tightly limited external market testing ahead of the first iPhone, and OpenAI chose a sudden public release of ChatGPT over more extensive testing. The price of market surprise: quality suffered. Strategic information asceticism (SIA) arises when a decision maker would strictly prefer to acquire information absent others’ strategic reactions yet forgoes it because others may exploit it once it exists. SIA is a two-sided phenomenon. The ascetic equilibrium holds because the decision maker’s restraint preserves uncertainty among sophisticated counterparts or unawareness among naïve ones. The analysis (i) defines SIA and distinguishes it from non-disclosure and strategic ignorance; (ii) develops a general model that yields testable comparative statics in leakage probability and opponent responsiveness; (iii) applies SIA to market testing as a canonical case; (iv) extends its application to espionage and test-optional college admissions; and (v) discusses governments countering SIA in regulatory settings. SIA differs sharply from well-known forms of information non-acquisition. It is not driven by internal factors such as processing costs, cognitive limitations, or preferences for ignorance. Neither does it involve selective disclosure or persuasion.

Irregular Demand: The Anti-Compromise Effect in the Field
Nicola Gennaioli et al.
NBER Working Paper, November 2026

Abstract:
Neoclassical demand obeys regularity: adding a good can only draw demand away from existing goods. In a natural field experiment with Lyft covering 7.2 million riders and 47 million choices, we randomize the presence and price of a premium ride. Contrary to regularity, the premium ride raises demand for the cheapest incumbent and for not buying. The effect grows with the premium price and with repeated exposure, and persists in sessions where the premium ride is not displayed. Rational inference and inattention cannot account for these facts. A model in which a surprisingly high price, cued on the app and retrieved from memory, draws attention to prices explains them.

Gaming the Marketplace: Consumer Opportunism and Beliefs about Societal Hierarchy
Shilpa Madan, Aparna Labroo & Constantine Katsikeas
Journal of Marketing Research, forthcoming

Abstract:
Consumers often behave opportunistically, taking more than what fair marketplace exchange warrants (e.g., taking excess samples, returning used items). While each individual transgression may be minor, cumulatively they can undermine firm profitability. Thus, addressing consumer opportunism is an important managerial concern. The authors identify a novel antecedent of consumer opportunism: consumers’ acceptance of societal hierarchy (i.e., power distance belief), including firms’ higher position in the hierarchy relative to consumers. Nine studies (plus two supplementary studies) employing archival, correlational, and experimental data provide converging evidence that, in marketplace interactions, this belief evokes a need to feel clever (i.e., to feel smart and knowledgeable vis-à-vis firms), which, in turn, promotes opportunistic behaviors. These behaviors exploit firm policy loopholes, allowing consumers to feel clever without explicitly defying firm authority. Higher-status consumers, who may be accustomed to a position of advantage and consequently less deferential, experience this need more, leading to greater opportunism. Reminders of surveillance reduce opportunism, but brand relationship reminders, paradoxically, license it. This research thus offers novel theoretical insights into consumer opportunism along with substantive managerial implications.

Celebrity-as-a-Service: Trust and Willingness to Use Digital Twins for Customer Service
Lingyao (Ivy) Yuan et al.
Journal of Management Information Systems, May 2026, Pages 335-367

Abstract:
A digital twin is an artificial intelligence (AI)- or human-controlled avatar that replicates a specific person’s identity. While organizations have used digital twins of employees (e.g. digital doctors answering patients’ questions), a more common use is celebrity-as-a-service, where digital twins of celebrities interact with customers. Unlike traditional celebrity endorsements in marketing videos, these digital-twin agents interact directly with consumers. Although digital twins do not enhance the underlying AI or human agents’ capabilities, their appearance as a specific person can influence users’ perception. Across two experiments, we found that when a digital twin resembled a celebrity, regardless of whether it was AI- or human-controlled, it was perceived to be more capable, benevolent, and trustworthy, leading to greater user engagement. Even when errors occurred, the celebrity’s likeness reduced negative reactions, suggesting that celebrity effects can buffer against algorithm aversion. Practically, digital celebrity twins offer business value comparable to traditional celebrity endorsements, influencing user trust and service adoption despite identical underlying performance.

Effects of land acknowledgements on non-Indigenous audiences in Australia and the USA
Lachlan McNamee & Kyle Peyton
Nature Human Behaviour, forthcoming

Abstract:
Land acknowledgements -- formal statements recognizing Indigenous custodianship of land -- are widespread in Australia, where they originated, and have been gaining traction in the USA. Proponents argue they raise awareness of Indigenous histories and build support for reparations, but causal evidence is limited. Here randomized experiments on non-Indigenous populations in Australia (N = 1,724) and the USA (N = 1,773) find that exposure to land acknowledgements increases awareness of local Indigenous groups but can reduce interest in Indigenous culture and heritage. We find no significant effects on a range of political attitudes, including collective guilt and support for reparations. Additional experiments (N = 3,638) suggest that the adoption of land acknowledgements provides small reputational benefits to institutions facing public scrutiny. Costlier practices -- such as financial compensation and Indigenous participation in decision-making -- have significantly larger effects. These findings suggest that land acknowledgements primarily improve organizational reputation rather than generate sociopolitical change.

item.title: Follow the Government Money — Taxing and spending
item.description:
The Marginal Net Taxation of Americans’ Labor Supply
David Altig et al.
Journal of Political Economy Macroeconomics, forthcoming

Abstract:
We assess how U.S. ﬁscal policies impact work incentives, using a life-cycle, consumption-smoothing program incorporating cash-ﬂow constraints and all major federal and state tax and beneﬁt policies. We calculate remaining lifetime marginal net tax rates (LMTRs), i.e., the present expected value of additional current and future taxes, net of beneﬁts, divided by a given increase in current labor earnings. One fourth of households in the bottom resource quintile face LMTRs above 45%. Those in the top 1% of the resource distribution face a median LMTR of 55%. We also ﬁnd remarkable dispersion in LMTRs and that double-taxation is signiﬁcant.

Can Government Support for Innovation Create the Next Silicon Valley?
Jason Baron, Shawn Kantor & Alexander Whalley
Journal of Economic Perspectives, Fall 2026, Pages 31-52

Abstract:
Can government support for innovation create the next Silicon Valley? We examine what public research and development can and cannot do to foster regional knowledge hubs. The historical record suggests that many successful hubs owe their origins partly to serendipity and favorable initial conditions. We then review causal evidence from universities, changes in intellectual property rules, new research institutions, wartime R&D, and the space race. Public R&D can raise local innovation, employment, and income, but the effects are heterogeneous, often modest relative to cost, and may partly reflect the relocation of firms and skilled workers from elsewhere. The evidence suggests a central role for complementary local inputs, including entrepreneurs, risk capital, skilled labor, firms, and institutions. Public R&D can help build a hub, but is unlikely to create one on its own.

One Big Beautiful Tax Shield: The Macroeconomics of Permanent Full Expensing
Doruk Gökalp
NYU Working Paper, November 2026

Abstract:
In July 2025, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made 100% equipment expensing permanent after two decades of temporary bonus depreciation. I evaluate this reform in a general-equilibrium heterogeneous-firm model with collateral constraints and nonrefundable tax deductions. When matched to U.S. tax-return and Compustat moments, the model yields three findings. First, permanent expensing raises long-run capital by 4.5% and output and real wages by 1.1%, roughly double the gains without financial frictions. Per present-value dollar of forgone corporate tax revenue, expensing builds 5.6 times as much capital as a tax rate cut, versus 3.4 times without financial frictions. Second, first-year capital purchases are U-shaped in firm age: young constrained firms and mature profitable firms expand, whereas unconstrained middle-aged firms whose investment exceeds taxable income delay purchases. Third, making expensing permanent gives up countercyclical bonus depreciation; enacted at the onset of a recession, a two-year bonus offsets 44% of the five-year investment drop.

Revisiting Retirement and Social Security Claiming Decisions
Neha Bairoliya & Kathleen McKiernan
Review of Economic Studies, forthcoming

Abstract:
The structure of the Social Security program presents a trade-off between benefit duration and size; individuals who claim early receive lower monthly payments. Surprisingly, even wealthy Americans with high life expectancies frequently claim benefits at the earliest eligibility age, a behavior inconsistent with conventional life-cycle theory predictions. In fact, there is a striking similarity in claiming ages across groups with vastly different life expectancies, wealth levels, and incentives to delay. This paper resolves this puzzle by introducing policy details and subjective beliefs about longevity and program rules into a rich, forward-looking life-cycle model. When included in the model, subjective beliefs substantially narrow the claiming-age gaps across education (college vs. non-college) and marital-status (married vs. single) groups. Specifically, differences in program beliefs alone account for 48.6% of the education claiming age gap and 75.1% of the marital status gap. Counterfactual policy simulations demonstrate that failing to account for these claiming mechanisms dramatically overstates individual responses to an increase in the normal retirement age and understates the resulting fiscal savings.

David Chavanne
Analyses of Social Issues and Public Policy, December 2026

Abstract:
This study uses survey responses to explore how support for basic income and universal healthcare is linked to zero-sum thinking and meritocratic beliefs. Consistent with earlier work, the results show that zero-sum thinking and weaker meritocratic beliefs are associated with increased support for basic income and universal healthcare. Zero-sum thinking and meritocratic beliefs are also associated with each other, with stronger zero-sum thinking corresponding with weaker meritocratic beliefs. These results suggest that zero-sum thinking plays an important role in shaping support for progressive policies, and that a multifaceted connection between zero-sum thinking and policy support may serve as a barrier to widespread recognition, appreciation, and promotion of the positive-sum consequences of these policies.

Do Voters Understand the Benefits of Taxes?
Benjamin Carter, Alessandro Del Ponte & Peter DeScioli
Perspectives on Politics, forthcoming

Abstract:
We use economic experiments to study a fundamental question in political economy: Do voters understand the benefits of taxes? Participants play an economic game as members of a virtual society composed of computer players. In each round, the players earn low or high income, see the distribution of income, and then vote for low or high taxes. We test whether participants vote rationally for high taxes when poor and low taxes when rich, following a classic model in political economy, or whether they focus on the burden of taxes more than the benefits. Across three experiments, poor players voted against high taxes 30% to 50% of the time, and they were more opposed when the same policy was labeled “taxes” than when it was labeled “sharing.” In Experiment 2, Singaporean participants opposed taxes at about the same rate as those of Americans in Experiment 1. In Experiment 3, participants’ opposition to taxes persisted when they received low income every round. These results support the burden hypothesis: voters focus more on the burden of paying taxes than on the benefits they provide. We reflect on what the results imply for the politics of taxes.

State and Local Government Review, forthcoming

Using a panel dataset of New Jersey municipalities, we analyze the association between local cannabis tax revenues and effective property tax rates. On average, a one dollar increase in local cannabis tax revenue per capita is associated with a statistically precise but substantively negligible 0.001 percentage point increase in effective property tax rates, suggesting that cannabis revenues do not meaningfully alter local property tax burdens. We also find little evidence that the association between cannabis revenues and effective property tax rates varies across municipalities with different levels of fiscal capacity or economic distress.

Journal of Marketing, forthcoming

Using market-level and transaction-level data from California, we show that lower-income consumers are less responsive to high-jackpot games, use random number generators less frequently, and favor popular number combinations. These behaviors interact with pari-mutuel prize structures to reduce expected earnings. Simulations indicate that these factors lead to approximately 7% higher losses per ticket for lower-income consumers, amounting to nearly $3 million annually. We evaluate alternative game formats and policy interventions -- including fixed non-jackpot prizes, mandatory random selection, and raffle-style jackpots with decreasing odds -- and find that they can reduce income-based disparities by up to 60%. By framing lottery products through the dimensions of function, ergonomics, and form, this research strengthens theoretical links between product design and consumer heterogeneity and offers actionable insights for policymakers seeking to design fairer games and more equitable consumer outcomes.
